blocks.text: Now, the statement that the stellio takes hold with its hands I refer either to its walking or to its hunting. For when it walks upside down, hanging from a ceiling, it must either fix its little claws in small cracks or clasp with its hands whatever projects or is rough. That it walks upside down is asserted in express words by the Philosopher in the History, book 9, chapter 9, where he speaks of the woodpecker thus: Πορεύεται ὕπτιος καθάπερ οἱ ἀσκαλαβῶται [poreuetai hyptios kathaper hoi askalabōtai]; It walks upside down like stellios. And in the Marvels: Τὸν δρυοκολάπτην τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπὶ τῶν δένδρων βαδίζειν φασὶν ὥσπερ τοὺς ἀσκαλαβώτας, καὶ ὕπτιον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν γαστέρα [ton dryokolaptēn to orneon epi tōn dendrōn badizein phasin hōsper tous askalabōtas, kai hyption, kai epi tēn gastera]; They say that the woodpecker walks on trees like stellios, upside down as well as face down. It is strange why Pliny renders ἀσκαλαβώτας [askalabōtas] as feles [cats], and ὕπτιον [hyption] as in subrectum [upright] instead of supinum [upside down], when he says in book 10, chapter 18, that the hollowers of trees (that is, δρυοκολάπτας [dryokolaptas], woodpeckers) climb upright in the manner of cats. All the more so since the same author, in book 29, chapter 4, acknowledges that the stellio is called in Greek colotes, ascalabotes and galeotes, so that no one should think Pliny was ignorant of the Greek names of the stellio. Similar is what we read in Plutarch's book On the Face in the Orb of the Moon: that what the geographers teach is highly paradoxical, ἀντίποδας οἰκεῖν, ὥσπερ θρίπας, ἢ γαλεώτας, τραπέντα ἄνω τὰ κάτω, τῇ γῇ προϊσχομένους [antipodas oikein, hōsper thripas, ē galeōtas, trapenta anō ta katō, tē gē proischomenous], that antipodes inhabit the earth, who, like woodworms or stellios, with the lower parts of their bodies turned upward, cling to the earth. Here likewise the first translators had written feles [cats] instead of stelliones.

We have also said that the stellio uses its hands for hunting, when it catches flies or spiders. Bustamantinus: It seizes with hands that promise security. Indeed the deceitful feet, which were bound to serve for motion, take the place of hands and carry out the plunder; and to it the feet on which it rests in moving are hands, and the hands with which it seizes its prey are feet. Rightly therefore Solomon says, The stellio takes hold with its hands, whether it walks upside down or throws itself upon its prey. Both are marvellous and most worthy of note in a tiny creature. The Greeks have here Καλαβώτης χερσὶν ἐρειδόμενος [Kalabōtēs chersin ereidomenos], and Jerome The stellio leans on its hands; the Arabic too has يتنسد بيديه [yatanassadu bi-yadayhi] it leans on its hands: as if referring this to walking. But no one could easily say what אקמתא דמסככה בידיה in the Chaldee means. For I do not [II, 519] understand what the Latin version means, The spider makes coverings with its hands. Nor much better is Gabriel, who rendered the same words of the Syriac paraphrase thus: The stellio, which creeps with its hands. I would rather read sepit [fences]; for סכך is to fence. But why the stellio should be said to fence, or to make coverings, I do not understand at all. Here too Drusius was at a loss in the Observations, book 10, chapter 6, and he suspects the passage of corruption. And instead of מסככה, fences or covers, he would sometimes read מסבכה, with Beth, entangling or making an intricate work, which would be said of the spider's web; sometimes מסמכה, leaning, which would be said of the stellio; so that the Chaldee would thus agree with the Greek and the Roman translators. But it is better to reconcile the Chaldee translator with the Hebrew text, in which תפש is to take hold. Accordingly Theodotion had rendered ἐλλαμβανόμενος [ellambanomenos]. I would therefore prefer to read, instead of מסככה mesacceca, מפככה mephacceca, Pe for Samech, letters not entirely dissimilar in shape. For פכך in Chaldee is the same as תפש in Hebrew, to take, to take hold. Thus Prov. V, 22. in the Venice edition: With the cords of his sins אתפכך, he is taken, or held fast.
